content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's definition — to judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a question or charge, with condemnation as the opposite — is the only supplied definition that carries every printed use of the word. The mainstream Protestant formulation ('God's forensic declaration that a sinner is righteous through faith in Christ') is true within Romans 3–5 but fails as the word's definition the moment the people 'justified God' (Luke 7:29), wisdom is 'justified of her children' (Matt 11:19), judges 'justify the righteous' (Deut 25:1), and men 'justify themselves' — a fact the common responses themselves concede by quarantining these as a separate 'demonstrative' sense. The book instead derives one courtroom sense (verdict against a charge) from Deut 25:1 and Prov 17:15 and shows it running unchanged through Paul (Rom 8:33 is explicitly accusation-language) and James. Its soteriological elaboration is likewise text-driven: Paul's own explanation of 'justifieth the ungodly' is David's forgiveness beatitude (Rom 4:5-8), so God answers the charge by forgiving through Christ's propitiation while remaining 'just, and the justifier' (Rom 3:26) — thereby satisfying Prov 17:15 rather than colliding with it. The strongest genuinely contradicting counter, the transformative make-righteous reading, cannot explain justifying God, justifying wisdom, judicial justification in Deut 25:1, or the false self-justifications of Luke 10:29 and 16:15 without equivocating on the word. Prior accepted findings on works (no wage-claim on God), works of the law (denial of purchase-power), righteousness (never renames wrong-living right), and faith directly establish the entry's secondary clauses. No supplied text is better explained by any counter than by the book.","book_core_identification":"To justify is to judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause to be right against a question or charge; its opposite is to condemn. It is a verdict-word, not a transformation-word, and the same sense governs every biblical use — judges justifying the righteous, men justifying themselves, people justifying God, wisdom justified by her children, and God justifying the believing sinner.","book_secondary_elaborations":["God's justification of the ungodly operates by grace through Christ's redemption and propitiation, answering the charge by forgiving and covering sin (Rom 3:24-26; 4:5-8) rather than by renaming ungodliness righteousness, so God remains just and the justifier and does not violate Prov 17:15.","Justification is received, not earned as a laborer's wage that would place God in debt (Rom 4:4-5; Luke 17:10).","Deeds may vindicate (demonstrate) a claimed faith — Abraham and Rahab in James 2 — but they cannot purchase the Judge's mercy; James's 'justified by works' is the demonstrative operation of the same verdict-word, not a rival purchase mechanism.","Justification is distinct from washing (removal of defilement) and sanctification (holy claim and appointment), per 1 Corinthians 6:11's three distinct verbs."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The transformative reading (Tridentine/Catholic, echoed in the Orthodox participation reading): dikaioō means that God actually makes the person righteous — an infusion of grace that inwardly renews and sanctifies, encompassing what Protestants call sanctification — so that justification is not merely a verdict concerning a charge but an effected moral and ontological change, evidenced by 1 Cor 6:11's placement of 'justified' alongside 'washed' and 'sanctified,' by Rom 5:19 ('many shall be made righteous'), and by James 2:24's insistence that works, not faith alone, justify.","counter_core_identification":"To justify is to make righteous: God's gracious act of inward transformation by which the sinner is actually rendered righteous, not merely declared or shown to be right against a charge.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The counter denies that 'justify' is a verdict-word at all: if justification is intrinsically a making-righteous by infused grace, then the book's identification of it as a judgment declared or demonstrated against a charge — capable of being rendered falsely, rendered toward God, or rendered by evidence — cannot be the word's meaning; the two cannot both be the core sense of the same verb.","counter_case":["1 Corinthians 6:11 lists 'justified' with 'washed' and 'sanctified' as things done to former sinners, suggesting real change rather than bare verdict.","Romans 5:19 says by one man's obedience 'many shall be made righteous,' language of effecting rather than declaring.","James 2:24 states flatly that 'by works a man is justified, and not by faith only,' fitting a justification that includes lived righteousness.","Prov 17:15 calls justifying the wicked an abomination; if God merely declared the still-wicked righteous, He would do what He condemns — so, the counter argues, God must actually make the person righteous.","The counter has massive traditional standing (Trent, patristic Greek readings), so it is not an eccentric construction."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["It alone carries the non-soteriological uses printed with the entry: judges justify the righteous (Deut 25:1), men justify the wicked falsely (Prov 17:15), wisdom is justified of her children (Matt 11:19), and the people justified God (Luke 7:29; cf. Rom 3:4) — God and wisdom cannot be made morally better, and a false verdict changes no one's character, so 'justify' must name a judgment, not a transformation.","It explains Rom 8:33 precisely: 'Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth' is accusation-and-verdict language, unintelligible as infusion language.","It resolves the Prov 17:15 problem without legal fiction: Paul's own gloss on 'justifieth the ungodly' is forgiveness — iniquities forgiven, sin not imputed (Rom 4:6-8) — so God answers the charge through Christ's propitiation (Rom 3:25-26) rather than declaring wickedness to be righteousness.","It harmonizes Paul and James with one definition: the same verdict-word operates declaratively before God (Rom 4:5) and demonstratively before evidence (Jas 2:21-25; Matt 12:37), so no equivocation or two-lexicon solution is required.","It integrates the accepted prior findings on works, works of the law, and righteousness: Rom 4:4-5 excludes the wage-claim, not obedience, exactly matching 'deeds cannot purchase the Judge's mercy.'","Its companion chapter keeps justify, sanctify, and cleanse distinct in 1 Cor 6:11, explaining why Paul used three verbs where one would do if all meant 'made spiritually better.'"],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Rom 5:19's 'made righteous' reads more naturally on the transformative view in isolation.","1 Cor 6:11's grouping of justified with washed and sanctified gives the counter a surface plausibility of real change.","The counter preserves an intuitive link between the verdict and actual moral renewal, avoiding any appearance of legal fiction — though the book achieves the same via forgiveness rather than infusion."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Deuteronomy 25:1 with Proverbs 17:15 — the paired courtroom definition and its abuse, fixing 'justify' as verdict opposed to 'condemn'","Luke 7:29 and Romans 3:4 — God is justified, ruling out any make-righteous meaning of the verb","Matthew 11:19 — wisdom justified by her children, the demonstrative operation of the same word","Romans 4:5-8 — Paul's own definition of justifying the ungodly as forgiveness and non-imputation of sin, quoting Psalm 32","Romans 8:33 — justification framed explicitly as answer to a laid charge","Romans 3:24-26 — God just and justifier through propitiation, resolving the Prov 17:15 tension","James 2:21-25 with 2:22-23 — works vindicating faith without purchasing mercy, unified under the same verdict-word"],"unresolved_objections":["Whether justification includes a positive imputation of Christ's righteousness as a distinct credit beyond forgiveness and non-imputation of sin (classic Protestant imputation) is a mechanism question the entry brackets; the printed texts (Rom 4:6-8) support the forgiveness framing, but 2 Cor 5:21 and Phil 3:9 were not adjudicated here.","The relation of justification to a future judgment 'according to works' (Rom 2:13; Matt 12:37) is touched (words justify or condemn) but not fully systematized in the entry.","Rom 5:19's 'made righteous' (katastathēsontai) receives no direct treatment in the supplied chapters, though it does not appear among the entry's printed references."],"confidence":"high"}
